entries.topicDescription: Understanding how Android creates, pauses, and destroys activities.

tips.title: The 6 lifecycle callbacks
tips.content:
Every Activity goes through: onCreate → onStart → onResume
(visible & interactive) and then onPause → onStop → onDestroy.

onCreate: initialize UI, set content view, restore saved state.
onStart: activity becomes visible but not yet interactive.
onResume: activity is in the foreground and receiving user input.
onPause: another activity is coming to the foreground.
onStop: activity is no longer visible.
onDestroy: activity is finishing or being destroyed by the system.

tips.title: Surviving configuration changes
tips.content:
When the user rotates the screen, Android destroys and recreates
the Activity. All local variables are lost.

Use ViewModel to hold UI state that must survive rotation.
Use onSaveInstanceState for small, serializable data.
Use rememberSaveable in Compose.

Never hold references to Activity or Context in a ViewModel —
the old Activity is destroyed but the ViewModel lives on,
causing a memory leak.

tips.title: LifecycleObserver for clean components
tips.content:
Instead of putting everything in Activity callbacks,
use LifecycleObserver to make self-contained components.

A LifecycleObserver watches lifecycle events independently.
This keeps your Activity clean and makes components reusable
across different Activities or Fragments.

The DefaultLifecycleObserver interface provides default
implementations for all lifecycle methods.

tips.title: onCreate, onStart, and onResume mark increasing degrees of visibility
tips.content:
onCreate runs once per instance for one-time setup (inflating views,
restoring saved state). onStart means the Activity is becoming visible but
may not have focus yet. onResume means it's fully visible and interactive
— this is where you should start anything that needs the UI actively in
the foreground, like camera previews or sensor listeners.

tips.title: onPause must be fast; onStop is where heavier cleanup belongs
tips.content:
onPause runs even when another Activity is only partially covering yours
(a dialog, a transparent Activity) — the system waits for it before
letting the new Activity fully resume, so slow work here visibly delays
the UI.

onStop only fires once your Activity is completely hidden, giving you
more headroom for heavier cleanup like unregistering listeners or pausing
video playback that doesn't need to stop the instant focus is lost.
tips.codeSnippet:
override fun onPause() { super.onPause(); saveDraftQuickly() } // must be fast
override fun onStop() { super.onStop(); unregisterSensorListener() } // heavier cleanup ok here

tips.title: Configuration changes destroy and recreate the Activity by default
tips.content:
A screen rotation, language change, or dark-mode toggle destroys the
current Activity instance and creates a brand new one by default — any
state held only in local variables or views is lost unless it's explicitly
saved and restored.

This is intentional: it lets the system re-select the correct resources
(layouts, strings, dimensions) for the new configuration by re-running
your setup code from scratch, rather than trying to patch an existing UI.
tips.codeSnippet:
// rotating the device by default triggers:
// onPause -> onStop -> onDestroy -> onCreate -> onStart -> onResume (new instance)

tips.title: onSaveInstanceState preserves transient UI state across recreation
tips.content:
Views handle their own simple state automatically (EditText text,
ScrollView position) if they have an ID, but anything held in your
Activity's own fields — a selected tab index, a temporary form draft —
needs to be saved manually.

onSaveInstanceState is called before the Activity is destroyed for
configuration changes or system-initiated destruction (not for user-
initiated back/finish), and the Bundle it fills is handed back in
onCreate's savedInstanceState parameter.

tips.title: ViewModel survives configuration changes, but not process death
tips.content:
A ViewModel scoped to an Activity or Fragment is retained across
configuration-change-triggered recreation — the same instance is handed
back, so in-memory state (loaded lists, network results) doesn't need to
be reloaded on rotation.

But ViewModel does NOT survive the system killing your process entirely
(e.g. to reclaim memory while your app is backgrounded) — for that
scenario, only data explicitly saved via SavedStateHandle or persisted to
disk survives.

tips.title: onDestroy isn't guaranteed to run — never rely on it for critical cleanup
tips.content:
When the system needs memory and kills a backgrounded process, it does so
without calling onDestroy at all — the process simply ends. Code that
relies on onDestroy for something essential (flushing unsaved data,
releasing a critical resource) can silently never run.

For anything that must happen reliably, use onPause or onStop instead
(which are much more reliably called before process death), or persist
state incrementally as it changes rather than batching it for a
destruction callback.

tips.title: isFinishing distinguishes user-initiated exit from a config-change destroy
tips.content:
onDestroy fires both when the user is genuinely leaving the Activity for
good (back press, finish()) and when it's being destroyed only to be
immediately recreated for a configuration change — treating both cases
identically can trigger unwanted cleanup during a routine rotation.

isFinishing() returns true only in the genuine-exit case, while
isChangingConfigurations() returns true specifically during a config-
change-triggered destroy — checking these lets onDestroy logic
differentiate the two situations.

tips.title: LifecycleObserver decouples lifecycle-aware logic from the Activity itself
tips.content:
Overriding every lifecycle callback in the Activity to manage an
unrelated component (a location tracker, an analytics session timer)
bloats the Activity with logic that isn't really about the Activity's own
UI.

Implementing DefaultLifecycleObserver on a separate class and registering
it via lifecycle.addObserver(...) lets that component react to lifecycle
events on its own, keeping the Activity's own callbacks focused only on
what's genuinely Activity-specific.

tips.title: Fragment lifecycle has its own states layered on top of the host Activity's
tips.content:
A Fragment's lifecycle isn't identical to its host Activity's — it adds
its own view-specific callbacks (onCreateView, onViewCreated,
onDestroyView) because a Fragment's underlying View can be destroyed and
recreated (e.g. when placed in a ViewPager) independently of the Fragment
object itself being destroyed.

This is why Fragment code must clean up view references in onDestroyView
specifically, not onDestroy — the Fragment instance can outlive its view,
and holding a stale view reference past onDestroyView is a common memory
leak source.

tips.title: onNewIntent fires instead of onCreate for singleTop/singleTask launches
tips.content:
When an Activity with launchMode singleTop or singleTask is relaunched
while an instance already exists at the top of the stack, Android reuses
that instance instead of creating a new one — onCreate does NOT run
again, and the new Intent is delivered via onNewIntent instead.

Forgetting to handle onNewIntent means data from the new launch (a fresh
deep link, a new notification payload) is silently ignored, since the
Activity's original Intent (from getIntent()) is unaffected unless you
explicitly call setIntent(intent) inside onNewIntent.

tips.title: View binding references must be nulled out to avoid leaking a destroyed view
tips.content:
Holding a ViewBinding reference in an Activity field is generally safe
since the Activity and its views share the same lifecycle — but in a
Fragment, the underlying View is destroyed in onDestroyView while the
Fragment object itself can live on, so a lingering binding reference
holds onto (and leaks) the destroyed View tree.

Always null out the Fragment's binding reference in onDestroyView, and
access it only through a getter that assumes it's non-null between
onCreateView and onDestroyView — a stray access outside that window
should crash loudly, not silently reference a stale view.

tips.title: Multi-window mode changes lifecycle assumptions — an Activity may stay resumed while partly hidden
tips.content:
In traditional single-window use, only one Activity is ever fully
resumed at a time. In split-screen or free-form multi-window mode, a
visible-but-not-focused Activity can remain in onResume rather than
dropping to onPause, since it's genuinely still visible to the user even
without input focus.

onMultiWindowModeChanged notifies you when the Activity enters or exits
multi-window mode, letting you adjust assumptions that previously relied
on 'resumed always means focused' being true.

tips.title: onRestart only fires when returning from a stopped, not paused, state
tips.content:
onRestart is easy to overlook because it doesn't fire on every return to
the Activity — only specifically when the Activity is coming back from
the stopped state (fully hidden, then revisited), not from paused (only
partially covered).

It always runs immediately before onStart in that specific transition, so
it's the right place for logic that should only re-run after a genuine
full hide-and-return, not after a brief partial obstruction like a
dialog.

tips.title: ActivityResultLauncher replaces the deprecated onActivityResult callback
tips.content:
The old startActivityForResult()/onActivityResult() pattern used a single
shared callback keyed by integer request codes, which got unwieldy and
error-prone as more result-producing calls were added to one Activity.

ActivityResultLauncher registers a dedicated, type-safe callback per
launch site at registration time (typically as a property, before
onCreate finishes), decoupling each result handler from a fragile shared
request-code switch statement.

tips.title: Process death loses everything not persisted, even ViewModel state
tips.content:
It's a common misconception that ViewModel alone is enough to survive
anything short of the user explicitly closing the app — but when the OS
kills your process to reclaim memory while backgrounded, the entire
process (including every ViewModel instance) is gone, and a fresh process
starts from scratch on return.

SavedStateHandle is specifically designed to survive this case — its data
is serialized to a small Bundle written to disk, separate from the
ViewModel instance itself, and restored into a new ViewModel when the
process restarts.

tips.title: Holding an Activity context beyond its lifecycle leaks the whole view tree
tips.content:
Passing `this` (an Activity context) into a long-lived singleton, a
static field, or a callback that outlives the Activity keeps the entire
Activity — and everything it references, including its full view
hierarchy — from being garbage collected even after the Activity is
destroyed.

Use applicationContext for anything that genuinely needs to outlive the
Activity (a singleton's initialization, for example), and prefer
WeakReference or lifecycle-scoped cleanup for callbacks that must
temporarily hold an Activity reference.

tips.title: Lifecycle.State is a snapshot; Lifecycle.Event is a transition
tips.content:
It's easy to conflate these two related but distinct concepts:
Lifecycle.State (CREATED, STARTED, RESUMED, etc.) represents where the
Activity currently sits, while Lifecycle.Event (ON_CREATE, ON_START,
ON_RESUME, etc.) represents the specific transition that just happened to
get there.

APIs like repeatOnLifecycle take a State (the condition to maintain),
while a LifecycleEventObserver's callback receives an Event (the moment-
in-time transition) — mixing these up is a common source of confusion
when implementing custom lifecycle-aware components.

tips.title: repeatOnLifecycle safely ties Flow collection to a lifecycle state, cancelling and restarting automatically
tips.content:
Launching a Flow collector directly in onCreate with lifecycleScope.launch
keeps collecting even when the Activity is stopped, wasting resources and
potentially processing stale UI updates against a backgrounded screen.

repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) automatically cancels the block
when the lifecycle drops below STARTED and restarts it when it comes back
above — this is the recommended pattern for collecting any Flow that
should only be active while the UI is visible.

tips.title: onTrimMemory signals memory pressure independently of the visible lifecycle callbacks
tips.content:
onPause/onStop tell you about visibility changes, but they say nothing
about system memory pressure — an Activity can stay fully resumed while
the system is under heavy memory pressure system-wide.

onTrimMemory delivers memory-pressure levels (from UI_HIDDEN through the
more severe COMPLETE/CRITICAL levels) so you can release caches or
nonessential resources proactively before the system is forced to kill
your process outright.

tips.title: Launch modes change how many lifecycle callback sequences you actually see
tips.content:
The default launchMode ("standard") always creates a brand new Activity
instance on every launch, running the full onCreate-through-onResume
sequence each time — even if an identical Activity is already on the
stack.

singleTop, singleTask, and singleInstance launch modes can instead reuse
an existing instance, replacing the full onCreate sequence with just
onNewIntent, onRestart, onStart, onResume for that reused instance — the
same code can execute a very different lifecycle sequence depending on
the launch mode declared in the manifest.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:launchMode="singleTop" />
<!-- relaunching while already on top skips onCreate — goes to onNewIntent instead -->

tips.title: Background execution limits interact with what an Activity can safely do while stopped
tips.content:
Once an Activity is stopped (fully backgrounded), the app as a whole is
subject to background execution limits (Doze mode, App Standby Buckets)
that can defer, batch, or restrict network access and wake locks — code
that assumes background work continues at full speed after onStop can
silently underperform or stall.

Work that must survive backgrounding reliably (sync, uploads) belongs in
WorkManager rather than in an Activity-scoped coroutine, since WorkManager
is specifically designed to cooperate with these system-level execution
restrictions.

tips.title: onWindowFocusChanged signals input focus, which is distinct from onResume's visibility
tips.content:
onResume means the Activity is on top of the task stack and interactive
in principle, but it doesn't guarantee actual keyboard/touch focus — a
system dialog, a notification shade pull-down, or picture-in-picture can
leave your Activity resumed but without window focus.

onWindowFocusChanged(hasFocus: Boolean) is the more precise signal for
'can the user currently interact with this window' — useful for pausing
time-sensitive interactions (game input, drawing) that should only run
while genuinely focused, not merely resumed.

tips.title: Predictive back gestures (Android 13+) introduce an in-progress, cancellable back state
tips.content:
Traditionally, a back press is a single atomic event — the system either
navigates back or it doesn't, with no in-between state visible to your
code. Predictive back introduces a gesture that can be previewed and
cancelled mid-swipe, meaning an Activity/Fragment can receive progress
callbacks for a back navigation that never actually completes.

OnBackPressedCallback's handleOnBackProgressed and
handleOnBackCancelled let you animate a preview of the destination and
revert cleanly if the user cancels the gesture, rather than assuming
every back signal is a completed, committed navigation.

tips.title: ActivityScenario lets tests drive lifecycle transitions explicitly
tips.content:
Manually simulating lifecycle transitions in an instrumented test (via
real user interaction or Robolectric shadow calls) is fragile and doesn't
reliably test how your Activity handles a specific transition in
isolation, like verifying state is preserved correctly across a
simulated rotation.

ActivityScenario (from androidx.test) lets a test explicitly move an
Activity through lifecycle states (moveToState, recreate()) and inspect
its behavior at each step, giving deterministic, repeatable coverage of
lifecycle-dependent logic without needing a real device rotation.
